claim: Jews have no religious or historical tie to this land; it is a Zionist invention.

heard.who: Mahmoud al-Habbash, adviser to the Palestinian Authority president, at a conference in Ramallah, June 2018 (as reported by The Algemeiner)
heard.quote: Palestine is not the (Jewish) Promised Land or the land of the (Jewish) forefathers

answer: The Quran does speak of the Children of Israel and a holy land. In 5:21 Moses tells his people to enter the holy land God has assigned to them. 7:137 says God made the oppressed Israelites heirs of blessed lands, 10:93 that He settled them in a blessed land, and 17:104 tells them to dwell in the land. So the text itself ties the Children of Israel to the land. Muslims read these verses differently. Classical commentators such as Ibn Kathir name Jerusalem, others Syria. In 5:22-26 the Israelites refuse and are barred for forty years, and the Azhar scholar Atiyyah Saqr held the promise lapsed with disobedience, while a few Muslim scholars read it as lasting. Jerusalem and al-Aqsa are sacred in Islam through the Night Journey and the first direction of prayer. Scripture alone does not settle who should govern the land today.

facts.text: Classical commentators agree that Moses ordered the Israelites to enter a holy land, but name different places: Ibn Kathir says Jerusalem, al-Jalalayn says Syria, and al-Tabari records several views (Sinai, Greater Syria, Jericho, Damascus with Palestine and part of Jordan).

sources.title: From the Commentary of Tabari (trans. Muhammad al-Hussaini)
sources.quote: others have said, "it is ash-Sham [Greater Syria]."

sources.title: Tafsirs for Quran 5.21 (Jalalayn)
sources.quote: which he commanded you to enter and this is Syria al-Shām

facts.text: Modern Muslim scholars read 5:21 differently. Some hold the promise was conditional or has lapsed (Atiyyah Saqr, former head of the Al-Azhar fatwa committee); some say the land was a temporary dwelling during the exodus, not an eternal homeland (a survey of contemporary commentators); and a few, such as Muhammad al-Hussaini, read the Quran as awarding the land to the Jews for all time.

sources.publisher: Journal of Eskişehir Osmangazi University Faculty of Theology
sources.title: Ersin Çelik, The Issue of the Promised Land from the Perspective of Classical and Modern Commentators (2025)
sources.quote: some exegetes argue that the land was given to the Israelites not as an eternal homeland but as a temporary dwelling during their exodus from Egypt

sources.title: Fatwa by Sheikh Atiyyah Saqr: Are the Jews the chosen people?
sources.quote: the promise stands so long as the people given this promise abide by Allah's teachings. Once they show disobedience, the promise no longer exists.

sources.title: Sahih al-Bukhari 1189
sources.quote: Do not set out on a journey except for three mosques i.e. Al-Masjid-ai-Haram

sources.title: Islam and Jerusalem
sources.quote: Jerusalem, which was the original qibla (direction of prayer) before it was changed to Mecca

contested: How the verses are read is a dispute inside Islam, not between Islam and outsiders. Çelik's survey finds exegetes disagree on the land's boundaries, that most classical commentators take the holy land to mean Jerusalem, and that contemporary commentators split into at least three approaches.

Robert Spencer, writing in Middle East Quarterly, argues that most Muslims cite other verses and hadith against a Jewish claim, that Islamic law has not accepted Jewish rule over the land, and that Hamas's charter calls Palestine an Islamic waqf (religious endowment). Al-Hussaini argues the opposite. Both essays appear on the Middle East Forum site, whose publisher takes a position on the conflict; the card uses it only for what each man says.

The Quran does not name Jerusalem; its 'farthest mosque' (17:1) is identified with Jerusalem by tradition. Al-Hussaini and Spencer both note that Jerusalem is not named in the Quran, and some Muslims have disputed the identification.
The Tabari excerpt was translated by al-Hussaini, who argues for the Jewish claim; the Tabari quote used here is a list of places, not his argument.

Whether a majority of living Muslim scholars hold the promise lapsed: no poll or survey was found. The card says only that Muslim scholars hold different views.
not_claimed: That scripture settles a modern political question: who should govern the land, or what borders, is not answered by the verses quoted.
That any reading of these verses is the correct Islamic one; the card reports what the text says and what Muslim scholars have said.
That the Israelites' tie to the land rests on the Quran: Jewish ties rest on Jewish sources and history (see the Jewish presence card).
That Muslim attachment to Jerusalem is weaker or newer because the Quran does not name the city.
